claim: Parkinson's disease is characterized by motor symptoms including tremor, bradykinesia, rigidity, postural instability, and freezing of gait.
source: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a complex neurodegenerative disorder characterized by non-motor manifestations and motor symptoms, including tremor, bradykinesia, rigidity, postural instability, and freezing of gait (Jankovic, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jankovic, 2008

claim: Dystonia is characterized by involuntary muscle contractions, repetitive movements, and abnormal fixed postures.
source: Dystonia is a movement disorder characterized by involuntary muscle contractions, repetitive movements, and abnormal fixed postures (Albanese et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Albanese et al., 2013

claim: Parkinson's disease is characterized as a collection of hypokinetic syndromes (apart from tremor and levodopa-induced dyskinesias).
source: While PD is characterized as a collection of hypokinetic syndromes (apart from tremor and levodopa-induced dyskinesias), dystonia is considered a hyperkinetic movement disorder.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the field

claim: Dystonia is considered a hyperkinetic movement disorder.
source: While PD is characterized as a collection of hypokinetic syndromes (apart from tremor and levodopa-induced dyskinesias), dystonia is considered a hyperkinetic movement disorder.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the field

claim: The dichotomy between the hypo- versus hyperkinetic nature of PD and dystonia is thought to be reflected in the underlying basal ganglia pathophysiology.
source: The dichotomy between the hypo- versus hyperkinetic nature of PD and dystonia, respectively, is thought to be reflected in the underlying basal ganglia pathophysiology.
evidence: Stated as a theoretical framework in the field

claim: Basal ganglia circuitry involves 'direct' (D1-mediated striatal projections to the internal globus pallidus [GPi]) and 'indirect' (D2-mediated striatal projections via the external globus pallidus and subthalamic nucleus to GPi) pathways.
source: In particular, basal ganglia circuitry that involves 'direct' (D1-mediated striatal projections to the internal globus pallidus [GPi]) and 'indirect' (D2-mediated striatal projections via the external globus pallidus and subthalamic nucleus to GPi) pathways has been implicated in these disorders (DeLong and Wichmann, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to DeLong and Wichmann, 2007

claim: In PD, activity in the indirect pathway is upregulated while the direct pathway is downregulated.
source: In PD, activity in the indirect pathway is upregulated while the direct pathway is downregulated, both of which converge toward increased GPi-mediated inhibition of thalamocortical motor networks (DeLong, 1990).
evidence: Supported by citation to DeLong, 1990

claim: In PD, upregulated indirect pathway activity and downregulated direct pathway activity converge toward increased GPi-mediated inhibition of thalamocortical motor networks.
source: In PD, activity in the indirect pathway is upregulated while the direct pathway is downregulated, both of which converge toward increased GPi-mediated inhibition of thalamocortical motor networks (DeLong, 1990).
evidence: Supported by citation to DeLong, 1990

claim: Dystonia has been hypothesized to occur as a result of hypofunctional indirect pathway activity.
source: Conversely, dystonia has been hypothesized to occur as a result of hypofunctional indirect pathway activity (Naumann et al., 1998; Simonyan et al., 2013) and/or hyperfunctional direct pathway activity (Simonyan et al., 2017), producing decreased GPi-mediated inhibition of thalamocortical motor networks.
evidence: Supported by citations to Naumann et al., 1998 and Simonyan et al., 2013

claim: Dystonia has been hypothesized to occur as a result of hyperfunctional direct pathway activity.
source: Conversely, dystonia has been hypothesized to occur as a result of hypofunctional indirect pathway activity (Naumann et al., 1998; Simonyan et al., 2013) and/or hyperfunctional direct pathway activity (Simonyan et al., 2017), producing decreased GPi-mediated inhibition of thalamocortical motor networks.
evidence: Supported by citation to Simonyan et al., 2017

claim: Dystonia produces decreased GPi-mediated inhibition of thalamocortical motor networks.
source: Conversely, dystonia has been hypothesized to occur as a result of hypofunctional indirect pathway activity (Naumann et al., 1998; Simonyan et al., 2013) and/or hyperfunctional direct pathway activity (Simonyan et al., 2017), producing decreased GPi-mediated inhibition of thalamocortical motor networks.
evidence: Inferred from the hypothesized pathway changes cited in the literature

claim: Circuit differences between PD and dystonia would result in increased GPi firing rates in PD and decreased rates in dystonia.
source: These circuit differences would thereby result in increased GPi firing rates (FRs) in PD and decreased rates in dystonia, which has been substantiated by some (Starr et al., 2005; Tang et al., 2007) but not all (Hutchison et al., 2003) human single-neuron studies.
evidence: Inferred from circuit models and supported by some citations (Starr et al., 2005; Tang et al., 2007) but contradicted by others (Hutchison et al., 2003)

claim: Some human single-neuron studies have substantiated increased GPi firing rates in PD and decreased rates in dystonia.
source: These circuit differences would thereby result in increased GPi firing rates (FRs) in PD and decreased rates in dystonia, which has been substantiated by some (Starr et al., 2005; Tang et al., 2007) but not all (Hutchison et al., 2003) human single-neuron studies.
evidence: Supported by citations to Starr et al., 2005 and Tang et al., 2007

claim: Not all human single-neuron studies have substantiated increased GPi firing rates in PD and decreased rates in dystonia.
source: These circuit differences would thereby result in increased GPi firing rates (FRs) in PD and decreased rates in dystonia, which has been substantiated by some (Starr et al., 2005; Tang et al., 2007) but not all (Hutchison et al., 2003) human single-neuron studies.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hutchison et al., 2003

claim: PD has been associated with increased beta (13–30 Hz) local field potential oscillations.
source: In addition to potential differences in single-neuron firing properties, each of the disorders has been associated with aberrant synchronization at the neural aggregate level; namely, increased beta (13–30 Hz) and theta (4–12 Hz) local field potential (LFP) oscillations in PD (Neumann et al., 2016) and dystonia (Neumann et al., 2017), respectively.
evidence: Supported by citation to Neumann et al., 2016

claim: Dystonia has been associated with increased theta (4–12 Hz) local field potential oscillations.
source: In addition to potential differences in single-neuron firing properties, each of the disorders has been associated with aberrant synchronization at the neural aggregate level; namely, increased beta (13–30 Hz) and theta (4–12 Hz) local field potential (LFP) oscillations in PD (Neumann et al., 2016) and dystonia (Neumann et al., 2017), respectively.
evidence: Supported by citation to Neumann et al., 2017

claim: Deep brain stimulation of the GPi is a widely used treatment for the motor symptoms of both PD and dystonia.
source: Despite opposing neurocircuit pathologies, deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the GPi is a widely used treatment for the motor symptoms of both PD and dystonia.
evidence: Stated as established clinical practice

claim: The timescales of symptomatic improvement after GPi-DBS are markedly longer in dystonia (minutes–hours–days) compared to PD (seconds–minutes).
source: However, the timescales of symptomatic improvement after GPi-DBS and the reappearance of symptoms upon stimulation cessation are markedly longer in dystonia (minutes–hours–days) compared to PD (seconds–minutes) (Stefani et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stefani et al., 2019

claim: The timescales of symptom reappearance upon stimulation cessation are markedly longer in dystonia (minutes–hours–days) compared to PD (seconds–minutes).
source: However, the timescales of symptomatic improvement after GPi-DBS and the reappearance of symptoms upon stimulation cessation are markedly longer in dystonia (minutes–hours–days) compared to PD (seconds–minutes) (Stefani et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stefani et al., 2019

claim: Differences in timescales of DBS effects may be the result of disease-specific dynamics of various forms of synaptic plasticity.
source: These differences in timescales may be the result of disease-specific dynamics of various forms of synaptic plasticity (Ruge et al., 2011a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ruge et al., 2011a

claim: High-frequency GPi stimulation induces synaptic depression of inhibitory striato-pallidal projections during stimulation in patients with PD.
source: Intriguingly, high-frequency GPi stimulation has been shown to induce synaptic depression of inhibitory striato-pallidal (GPi) projections during stimulation (short-term plasticity effects), followed by an enduring potentiation of these projections after stimulation cessation (long-term plasticity-like effects) in both patients with PD (Milosevic et al., 2019) and dystonia (Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Milosevic et al., 2019

claim: High-frequency GPi stimulation induces synaptic depression of inhibitory striato-pallidal projections during stimulation in patients with dystonia.
source: Intriguingly, high-frequency GPi stimulation has been shown to induce synaptic depression of inhibitory striato-pallidal (GPi) projections during stimulation (short-term plasticity effects), followed by an enduring potentiation of these projections after stimulation cessation (long-term plasticity-like effects) in both patients with PD (Milosevic et al., 2019) and dystonia (Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2012

claim: High-frequency GPi stimulation induces enduring potentiation of striato-pallidal projections after stimulation cessation in patients with PD.
source: Intriguingly, high-frequency GPi stimulation has been shown to induce synaptic depression of inhibitory striato-pallidal (GPi) projections during stimulation (short-term plasticity effects), followed by an enduring potentiation of these projections after stimulation cessation (long-term plasticity-like effects) in both patients with PD (Milosevic et al., 2019) and dystonia (Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Milosevic et al., 2019

claim: High-frequency GPi stimulation induces enduring potentiation of striato-pallidal projections after stimulation cessation in patients with dystonia.
source: Intriguingly, high-frequency GPi stimulation has been shown to induce synaptic depression of inhibitory striato-pallidal (GPi) projections during stimulation (short-term plasticity effects), followed by an enduring potentiation of these projections after stimulation cessation (long-term plasticity-like effects) in both patients with PD (Milosevic et al., 2019) and dystonia (Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2012

claim: Data were collected from 19 patients with non-genetic dystonia (135 included segments) for the single-neuron feature analysis.
source: For the single-neuron feature analysis (Figure 1), data were collected from 19 patients with non-genetic dystonia (135 included segments; see Supplementary file 1 for information on subtypes) and 44 patients with PD (222 segments) during awake microelectrode-guided GPi-DBS surgeries (Hutchison et al., 1994) after overnight withdrawal of anti-Parkinsonian medications in patients with PD.
evidence: Describes the data collection methodology

claim: Data were collected from 44 patients with PD (222 segments) for the single-neuron feature analysis.
source: For the single-neuron feature analysis (Figure 1), data were collected from 19 patients with non-genetic dystonia (135 included segments; see Supplementary file 1 for information on subtypes) and 44 patients with PD (222 segments) during awake microelectrode-guided GPi-DBS surgeries (Hutchison et al., 1994) after overnight withdrawal of anti-Parkinsonian medications in patients with PD.
evidence: Describes the data collection methodology

claim: Data were collected during awake microelectrode-guided GPi-DBS surgeries after overnight withdrawal of anti-Parkinsonian medications in patients with PD.
source: For the single-neuron feature analysis (Figure 1), data were collected from 19 patients with non-genetic dystonia (135 included segments; see Supplementary file 1 for information on subtypes) and 44 patients with PD (222 segments) during awake microelectrode-guided GPi-DBS surgeries (Hutchison et al., 1994) after overnight withdrawal of anti-Parkinsonian medications in patients with PD.
evidence: Describes the data collection methodology

claim: For plasticity analyses, data were collected from a subset of 8 patients with dystonia (12 recording sites).
source: For plasticity analyses (Figure 2), data were collected from a subset of 8 patients with dystonia (12 recording sites) and 10 patients with PD (13 recording sites).
evidence: Describes the data collection methodology

claim: For plasticity analyses, data were collected from 10 patients with PD (13 recording sites).
source: For plasticity analyses (Figure 2), data were collected from a subset of 8 patients with dystonia (12 recording sites) and 10 patients with PD (13 recording sites).
evidence: Describes the data collection methodology

claim: GPi neurons exhibited lower firing rates in dystonia compared to PD.
source: In dystonia, FR was lower (MWU test; p=0.0252) and neurons were bustier (higher BI; MWU test; p=0.0024) and less regular (higher CV; MWU test; p<0.0001) compared to PD (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (Mann-Whitney U test) of experimental data shown in Figure 1A

claim: GPi neurons were bustier (higher burst index) in dystonia compared to PD.
source: In dystonia, FR was lower (MWU test; p=0.0252) and neurons were bustier (higher BI; MWU test; p=0.0024) and less regular (higher CV; MWU test; p<0.0001) compared to PD (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (Mann-Whitney U test) of experimental data shown in Figure 1A

claim: GPi neurons were less regular (higher coefficient of variation) in dystonia compared to PD.
source: In dystonia, FR was lower (MWU test; p=0.0252) and neurons were bustier (higher BI; MWU test; p=0.0024) and less regular (higher CV; MWU test; p<0.0001) compared to PD (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (Mann-Whitney U test) of experimental data shown in Figure 1A

claim: There were no significant differences in spiketrain oscillations in the delta frequency band between PD and dystonia.
source: However, there were no significant differences in spiketrain oscillations in the delta (MWU test; p=0.6265), theta (MWU test; p=0.3649), low-beta (MWU test; p=0.1176), or high-beta (MWU test; p=0.4585) frequency bands (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (Mann-Whitney U test) of experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: There were no significant differences in spiketrain oscillations in the theta frequency band between PD and dystonia.
source: However, there were no significant differences in spiketrain oscillations in the delta (MWU test; p=0.6265), theta (MWU test; p=0.3649), low-beta (MWU test; p=0.1176), or high-beta (MWU test; p=0.4585) frequency bands (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (Mann-Whitney U test) of experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: There were no significant differences in spiketrain oscillations in the low-beta frequency band between PD and dystonia.
source: However, there were no significant differences in spiketrain oscillations in the delta (MWU test; p=0.6265), theta (MWU test; p=0.3649), low-beta (MWU test; p=0.1176), or high-beta (MWU test; p=0.4585) frequency bands (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (Mann-Whitney U test) of experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: There were no significant differences in spiketrain oscillations in the high-beta frequency band between PD and dystonia.
source: However, there were no significant differences in spiketrain oscillations in the delta (MWU test; p=0.6265), theta (MWU test; p=0.3649), low-beta (MWU test; p=0.1176), or high-beta (MWU test; p=0.4585) frequency bands (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (Mann-Whitney U test) of experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: The firing rate difference between PD and dystonia did not survive Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons.
source: The post hoc Bonferroni correction (adjusted significance threshold to p<0.0071) indicated that FR difference between PD and dystonia did not survive multiple comparisons (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Statistical analysis with multiple comparison correction

claim: In dystonia, symptom severity negatively correlated with firing rate.
source: In dystonia, symptom severity negatively correlated with FR (Spearman's rho = −0.49, p=0.0370) and positively correlated with CV (Spearman's rho = 0.48, p=0.0364; Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by Spearman correlation analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: In dystonia, symptom severity positively correlated with coefficient of variation.
source: In dystonia, symptom severity negatively correlated with FR (Spearman's rho = −0.49, p=0.0370) and positively correlated with CV (Spearman's rho = 0.48, p=0.0364; Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by Spearman correlation analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: In PD, symptom severity positively correlated with low beta spiketrain oscillations.
source: For oscillatory spiketrain features, symptom severity positively correlated with low beta in PD (Spearman's rho = 0.30, p=0.0426), with a marginally stronger correlation for PD hypokinetic symptoms only (items 23–26 of UPDRSIII, Spearman's rho = 0.32, p=0.0330; Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and theta in dystonia (Spearman's rho = 0.51, p=0.0242; Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by Spearman correlation analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: In PD, hypokinetic symptom severity positively correlated with low beta spiketrain oscillations with a marginally stronger correlation than total symptom severity.
source: For oscillatory spiketrain features, symptom severity positively correlated with low beta in PD (Spearman's rho = 0.30, p=0.0426), with a marginally stronger correlation for PD hypokinetic symptoms only (items 23–26 of UPDRSIII, Spearman's rho = 0.32, p=0.0330; Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and theta in dystonia (Spearman's rho = 0.51, p=0.0242; Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by Spearman correlation analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: In dystonia, symptom severity positively correlated with theta spiketrain oscillations.
source: For oscillatory spiketrain features, symptom severity positively correlated with low beta in PD (Spearman's rho = 0.30, p=0.0426), with a marginally stronger correlation for PD hypokinetic symptoms only (items 23–26 of UPDRSIII, Spearman's rho = 0.32, p=0.0330; Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and theta in dystonia (Spearman's rho = 0.51, p=0.0242; Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by Spearman correlation analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: None of the clinical correlations survived Benjamini–Hochberg FDR correction for multiple comparisons.
source: However, none of the clinical correlations survived Benjamini–Hochberg FDR correction for multiple comparisons (Supplementary file 3b).
evidence: Statistical analysis with multiple comparison correction

claim: In PD, fEP amplitudes were significantly greater after compared to before HFS.
source: In PD, fEP amplitudes were significantly greater after compared to before HFS (LMM; p=0.0075, effect size = 5.42 ± 1.79; Figure 2C), while in dystonia, the increase approached but did not reach statistical significance (LMM; p=0.0708, effect size = 2.82 ± 1.45; Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by linear mixed model analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2C

claim: In dystonia, the increase in fEP amplitudes after compared to before HFS approached but did not reach statistical significance.
source: In PD, fEP amplitudes were significantly greater after compared to before HFS (LMM; p=0.0075, effect size = 5.42 ± 1.79; Figure 2C), while in dystonia, the increase approached but did not reach statistical significance (LMM; p=0.0708, effect size = 2.82 ± 1.45; Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by linear mixed model analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2C

claim: The percent change in fEP amplitude was significantly greater in PD compared to dystonia.
source: The percent change in fEP amplitude was significantly greater in PD compared to dystonia (LMM; p=0.0396, effect size = 12.40 ± 5.41; Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by linear mixed model analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2D

claim: Half-life values extracted from double exponential fits on the first five fEPs during HFS were significantly greater in dystonia compared to PD.
source: Half-life values extracted from double exponential fits on the first five fEPs during HFS were significantly greater in dystonia compared to PD (LMM; p=0.0139, effect size = 1.04 ± 0.37; Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by linear mixed model analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2G

claim: The findings substantiate claims of hypofunctional GPi output in dystonia.
source: In this work, we leveraged the intraoperative environment to characterize GPi spiketrain features and to record and manipulate the efficacy of inhibitory direct pathway striato-pallidal projections in order to derive insights about disease-related features of basal ganglia circuit function in PD and dystonia. In particular, we found that GPi neurons exhibited lower FRs, but greater burstiness and variability in dystonia compared to PD (Figure 1A).
evidence: Inferred from the experimental findings of lower firing rates in dystonia

claim: The findings substantiate claims of hyperfunctional GPi output in PD.
source: In this work, we leveraged the intraoperative environment to characterize GPi spiketrain features and to record and manipulate the efficacy of inhibitory direct pathway striato-pallidal projections in order to derive insights about disease-related features of basal ganglia circuit function in PD and dystonia. In particular, we found that GPi neurons exhibited lower FRs, but greater burstiness and variability in dystonia compared to PD (Figure 1A).
evidence: Inferred from the experimental findings of higher firing rates in PD compared to dystonia

claim: The findings provide cellular-level validation of the pathological nature of low-beta oscillations in PD.
source: While no differences were found in the power of spiketrain oscillations across disorders (Figure 1B), we found that PD symptom severity positively correlated with the power of low-beta frequency spiketrain oscillations, whereas dystonia symptom severity positively correlated with the power of theta frequency spiketrain oscillations (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis between single-neuron oscillations and clinical severity

claim: The findings provide cellular-level validation of the pathological nature of theta oscillations in dystonia.
source: While no differences were found in the power of spiketrain oscillations across disorders (Figure 1B), we found that PD symptom severity positively correlated with the power of low-beta frequency spiketrain oscillations, whereas dystonia symptom severity positively correlated with the power of theta frequency spiketrain oscillations (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis between single-neuron oscillations and clinical severity

claim: Circuit changes in PD and dystonia may be underlain by disease-related differences in plasticity of striato-pallidal synapses.
source: These results are discussed in greater detail with respect to previous literature in the section 'Neuronal correlates of PD and dystonia'. In response to electrical stimulation (protocol depicted in Figure 2A), we found significant increases in the amplitudes of positive-going stimulation-evoked field potential amplitudes (considered to reflect striato-pallidal synaptic strength, as exemplified in Figure 2B) before versus after HFS in both PD and dystonia (Figure 2C), with recording sites in PD exhibiting significantly greater increases (Figure 2D).
evidence: Inferred from the experimental findings of differences in plasticity between disorders

claim: Dystonia is associated with less long-term plasticity compared to PD.
source: Dystonia was moreover associated with less long-term plasticity and slower synaptic depression.
evidence: Supported by experimental data on fEP amplitude changes

claim: Dystonia is associated with slower synaptic depression compared to PD.
source: Dystonia was moreover associated with less long-term plasticity and slower synaptic depression.
evidence: Supported by experimental data on fEP dynamics during HFS

claim: Lower firing rates in dystonia may substantiate claims of greater inhibition of GPi producing decreased inhibitory output and under-inhibition of thalamocortical motor networks.
source: To this end, our findings (Figure 1A) of lower FRs in dystonia compared to PD may further substantiate (Starr et al., 2005; Tang et al., 2007) such claims, whereby greater inhibition of GPi would produce decreased inhibitory output, and thus under-inhibition of thalamocortical motor networks, giving rise to hyperkinetic motor symptoms, whereas the opposite would be true in PD (DeLong and Wichmann, 2007).
evidence: Inferred from experimental findings and supported by citations

claim: GPi neuronal firing rates may not directly correlate with motor severity in PD but exhibit variability across the disease severity continuum.
source: Despite the lack of correlations with FR in PD, our findings seem to align with those of Muralidharan and colleagues (Muralidharan et al., 2016), who showed that GPi neuronal FRs may not directly correlate with motor severity but exhibit variability across the disease severity continuum in Parkinsonian non-human primates (initially increasing, then decreasing, then increasing again at mild, moderate, and severe disease manifestations, respectively).
evidence: Supported by citation to Muralidharan et al., 2016

claim: Pathological oscillations at the neural aggregate/LFP level are likely encoded by periodic oscillations in the firing rates of single neurons.
source: From a neural synchronization standpoint, we recently showed that pathological oscillations at the neural aggregate/LFP level are likely encoded by periodic oscillations in the FRs of single neurons (Scherer et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Scherer et al., 2022

claim: A study in non-human primates found no differences in single-neuron oscillatory strength between PD and dystonia.
source: Although previous research has reported differences in the LFP power between PD and dystonia (Silberstein et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2018), a study in non-human primates found no such differences in single-neuron oscillatory strength (Starr et al., 2005), as reflected in our findings.
evidence: Supported by citation to Starr et al., 2005

claim: The amplitude of positive-going inhibitory fEPs is directly associated with the duration of neuronal inhibition.
source: We have previously shown that the amplitude of positive-going inhibitory fEPs is directly associated with the duration of neuronal inhibition Milosevic et al., 2019; Steiner et al., 2021, thus serving as a viable substrate of inhibitory synaptic transmission efficacy.
evidence: Supported by citations to Milosevic et al., 2019 and Steiner et al., 2021

claim: Both positive-going extracellular fields and neuronal inhibition are reversed with the application of GABA antagonists in animals.
source: These observations are supported by work in animals demonstrating the reversal of both positive-going extracellular fields and neuronal inhibition with the application of GABA antagonists (Yoshida and Precht, 1971; Precht and Yoshida, 1971).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yoshida and Precht, 1971 and Precht and Yoshida, 1971

claim: Low-latency inhibitory fields recorded in the subthalamic nucleus (GPe-mediated) are far smaller in amplitude and are resilient during HFS.
source: Importantly, we previously Steiner et al., 2021 demonstrated that low-latency inhibitory fields recorded in the subthalamic nucleus (GPe-mediated) are far smaller in amplitude and are resilient during HFS (i.e., minimal synaptic depression), whereas high-latency inhibitory fields recorded in substantia nigra pars reticulata and GPi (Liu et al., 2012) (striatum-mediated) are far larger in amplitude and are subject to potent synaptic depression during HFS, thus, enabling electrophysiological discernment of these distinct inhibitory projections in humans.
evidence: Supported by citation to Steiner et al., 2021

claim: High-latency inhibitory fields recorded in substantia nigra pars reticulata and GPi (striatum-mediated) are far larger in amplitude and are subject to potent synaptic depression during HFS.
source: Importantly, we previously Steiner et al., 2021 demonstrated that low-latency inhibitory fields recorded in the subthalamic nucleus (GPe-mediated) are far smaller in amplitude and are resilient during HFS (i.e., minimal synaptic depression), whereas high-latency inhibitory fields recorded in substantia nigra pars reticulata and GPi (Liu et al., 2012) (striatum-mediated) are far larger in amplitude and are subject to potent synaptic depression during HFS, thus, enabling electrophysiological discernment of these distinct inhibitory projections in humans.
evidence: Supported by citations to Steiner et al., 2021 and Liu et al., 2012

claim: Dystonia is associated with impaired synaptic function and abnormal synaptic plasticity.
source: Converging evidence from past animal and human studies suggests that dystonia is associated with impaired synaptic function and abnormal synaptic plasticity (Chen and Udupa, 2009; Peterson et al., 2010; Quartarone and Pisani, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen and Udupa, 2009; Peterson et al., 2010; Quartarone and Pisani, 2011

claim: Transcranial magnetic stimulation-induced motor-evoked potentials are hyperexcitable in dystonia compared to healthy controls.
source: Compared to healthy controls, it has been shown that transcranial magnetic stimulation-induced motor-evoked potentials are hyperexcitable in dystonia Chen, 2000; Siebner et al., 1999, and somatosensory and motor cortical plasticity is greater (Tamura et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen, 2000 and Siebner et al., 1999

claim: Somatosensory and motor cortical plasticity is greater in dystonia compared to healthy controls.
source: Compared to healthy controls, it has been shown that transcranial magnetic stimulation-induced motor-evoked potentials are hyperexcitable in dystonia Chen, 2000; Siebner et al., 1999, and somatosensory and motor cortical plasticity is greater (Tamura et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tamura et al., 2009

claim: Enhanced long-term potentiation at cortico-striatal synapses has been shown in rodent models of dystonia.
source: Likewise, enhanced long-term potentiation at cortico-striatal synapses has been shown in rodent models of dystonia (Köhling et al., 2004; Martella et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Köhling et al., 2004 and Martella et al., 2009

claim: All patients with PD in this study are long-term users of levodopa.
source: While our finding that long-term potentiation effects are greater in PD compared to dystonia (Figure 2D) is difficult to corroborate with this literature, one potential explanation can be that all of our patients with PD are long-term users of levodopa.
evidence: Stated as a characteristic of the patient cohort

claim: The intake of levodopa leads to potent increases in the magnitude of direct pathway plasticity.
source: We have previously shown that the intake of this antiparkinsonian dopaminergic medication leads to potent increases in the magnitude of direct pathway plasticity (Milosevic et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Milosevic et al., 2019

claim: Striato-pallidal synapses may be chronically over-sensitized from prolonged use of dopaminergic medication in PD patients.
source: Although patients are 12 hr withdrawn from anti-Parkinsonian medications for surgery, it could be that striato-pallidal synapses are nevertheless chronically over-sensitized from prolonged use of dopaminergic medication, which is a well-known hypothesis related to the manifestation of levodopa-induced dyskinesias (a hyperkinetic feature) in PD (Calabresi et al., 2015).
evidence: Speculative inference supported by citation to Calabresi et al., 2015

claim: A lack of depotentiation of striato-pallidal projections has been observed in patients with levodopa-induced dyskinesias.
source: Indeed, a lack of depotentiation of striato-pallidal projections has previously been observed in patients with levodopa-induced dyskinesias (Prescott et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Prescott et al., 2014

claim: Excessive plasticity of striato-pallidal projections may corroborate hyperkinetic features of dystonia and levodopa-induced dyskinesias in PD.
source: As such, excessive plasticity of these projections may corroborate hyperkinetic features of dystonia and levodopa-induced dyskinesias in PD.
evidence: Speculative inference from the experimental findings

claim: DBS in dystonia leads to more rapid improvement in the transient, dynamic muscle contractions (phasic components) compared to the sustained, continuous muscle contractions (tonic or fixed components).
source: Clinical studies in dystonia have shown that DBS leads to a more rapid improvement in the transient, dynamic muscle contractions (phasic components) of the disorder compared to the sustained, continuous muscle contractions (tonic or fixed components) (Krauss, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Krauss, 2002

claim: The early improvement of the phasic component in dystonia has been suggested to be associated with direct suppression of abnormal activity in the GPi.
